info.title: timr API
info.description:
The timr REST API enables you to integrate timr with your own applications, services and business processes.

Use the API to access supported resources such as **working times, absences, project times, drive logs and related master data**. Depending on the resource, the API provides **read and/or write access**.

## Integrate timr with your systems

API access can operate either on **client level**, across the organization, or within the permissions of an individual **timr user**.

For integrations that replicate timr data into another system, the API supports **efficient incremental synchronization**, including access to changed and deleted records.

### Typical use cases

The timr REST API can be used to:

- **Synchronize timr data with external applications**
- **Import or update supported data in timr**
- **Build custom reports and dashboards**
- **Replicate timr data into your own systems**

## Need help or missing an endpoint?

If you have questions about the API, need help with your integration, or require access to data or functionality that is currently not available through the API, please contact our [support team](https://www.timr.com/en/s/support/). We’re happy to review your use case and available options.

tags.name: Authentication
tags.description:
Integrations authenticate with OAuth2. Rather than handling a timr username and password, your
application obtains an access token from the timr authorization server and sends it with every
request:

```http
GET /v1/working-times HTTP/1.1
Host: api.timr.com
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

A request without a valid token is answered with `401 Unauthorized`.

## Choosing a flow

Which flow you use depends on whose data your integration touches.

**Client credentials** suits a system talking to timr as itself — a nightly export, a sync job, a
service reconciling timr with another system. The token is issued for the client and grants access in
the client context, across users, according to the permissions the client has. No person signs in and
no browser is involved.

**Authorization code** suits an integration acting on behalf of an individual timr user — a desktop
tool, a mobile app, anything where someone signs in and works with their own data. The token is
issued in the context of that user and is limited to that user's permissions; it does not grant
account-wide access. Add the `offline_access` scope to receive a refresh token as well.

## Creating API credentials

You need to be a timr administrator.

Open **Administration → Settings → Integrations**, and under **API Credentials** click **+ Add**.
Give the client a name, choose its grant type, and save. timr then shows the client ID, and for a
confidential client the client secret — which is displayed only there, so store it securely.

## Finding the endpoints

The authorization server publishes its OpenID Provider metadata:

```
https://system.timr.com/id/.well-known/openid-configuration
```

Read the authorization and token endpoints from that document rather than hardcoding them, so an
endpoint can move without breaking your integration. Today they are:

|                        |                                               |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Authorization endpoint | `https://system.timr.com/id/oauth2/authorize` |
| Token endpoint         | `https://system.timr.com/id/oauth2/token`     |
| API base URL           | `https://api.timr.com/v1`                     |

An unauthenticated response also points at the metadata describing this API, following
[RFC 9728](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728.html), which names the authorization server that
protects it:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.timr.com/v1/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
```

## Client credentials

Client credentials clients use the scopes `openid timrclient`. Request a token from the token
endpoint:

```http
POST /id/oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Host: system.timr.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=<client_id>&client_secret=<client_secret>&grant_type=client_credentials&scope=openid timrclient
```

```json
{
  "access_token": "<access_token>",
  "scope": "openid timrclient",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3599
}
```

This flow returns no refresh token. When the access token expires, repeat the same request.

## Authorization code

Authorization code clients use the scopes `openid offline_access`.

### Redirect URLs

Configure at least one redirect URL on the client. They must be absolute and must not contain a
fragment, one per line:

```
https://example.com/oauth/timr/callback
https://app.example.com/integrations/timr/callback
```

The `redirect_uri` you send in the authorization and token requests must match one of them exactly,
so register every URL you use — including the one you develop against.

### Step 1 — send the user to the authorization endpoint

```http
GET /id/oauth2/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=<client_id>&redirect_uri=<redirect_uri>&scope=openid%20offline_access&state=<state> HTTP/1.1
Host: system.timr.com
```

Generate `state` yourself, store it before redirecting, and verify it when the user comes back — it
is what protects the callback from being forged. After signing in, the user is returned to your
redirect URL:

```
https://example.com/oauth/timr/callback?code=<authorization_code>&state=<state>
```

### Step 2 — exchange the code for tokens

```http
POST /id/oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Host: system.timr.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=<client_id>&client_secret=<client_secret>&grant_type=authorization_code&code=<authorization_code>&redirect_uri=<redirect_uri>
```

```json
{
  "access_token": "<access_token>",
  "refresh_token": "<refresh_token>",
  "scope": "openid offline_access",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3599
}
```

### Step 3 — refresh when the token expires

```http
POST /id/oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Host: system.timr.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=<client_id>&client_secret=<client_secret>&grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=<refresh_token>
```

If the response carries a new refresh token, replace the one you stored.

### Public clients and PKCE

An application that cannot keep a secret — anything running on a user's device or in a browser — is
a public client. It must not embed a client secret, and secures the flow with PKCE instead: send a
`code_challenge` with the authorization request and the matching `code_verifier` with the token
request, and omit `client_secret` entirely.

## Troubleshooting

**The authorization request is rejected.** Check that `redirect_uri` matches a configured URL
exactly, that it is absolute, and that it has no fragment.

**No refresh token came back.** Refresh tokens are issued only by the authorization code flow, and
only when `offline_access` is among the requested scopes.

**A request returns fewer entries than expected.** Each endpoint returns only what the authenticated
user or client may see, so an empty list can mean a missing permission rather than missing data.
Requesting something that exists but is not visible to you is answered with `403 Forbidden`.

## Trying it out

The **Authorize** button at the top of this page runs the authorization code flow with PKCE for you.
Enter your client ID, choose the scopes, and the requests you send from any endpoint below carry the
resulting token — register this page's URL as a redirect URL on the client you use here.

tags.name: Identifiers
tags.description:
Every entry the API returns is identified by an `id`, and identifiers are **opaque strings**. Their
format is not part of this contract: do not parse them, derive meaning from them, sort by them, or
assume how long they are. Store them as text, and pass them back unchanged.

```json
{
  "id": "7e05c860-2793-4e0b-938e-5a5641fc981c",
  "external_id": "PAY-2026-00417"
}
```

## Your own identifiers

Fields named `external_id` are yours. They hold the identifier an object has in your system — a
payroll number, a row key, a ticket reference — and timr only stores and returns them. You decide
the format, and you decide whether to set one at all.

They are how you recognise your own records when they come back: write your identifier when you
create the entry, and every later read carries it.

Note that no endpoint filters by `external_id` — you cannot ask timr for the entry with a given one.
An integration that needs to look entries up by its own identifier has to keep the mapping, or fetch
the page it expects and match on the way through.

tags.name: Dates and times
tags.description:
Date-time values follow [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html), the internet profile
of [ISO 8601](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html), and always carry an explicit
UTC offset:

```
2021-07-16T09:30:00+02:00
```

Plain dates are `YYYY-MM-DD` and carry no time and no zone:

```
2021-07-16
```

## A date without a year

Something that recurs every year has no year to state, and those fields use the ISO 8601 month-day
form. The leading double hyphen is part of it — it is how ISO 8601 marks a representation with the
year omitted, and a value without it is rejected:

```
--05-20
```

`User.vacation_year_start` is the one field of this kind today: the month and day on which a user's
vacation year begins, which is the same date every year. Read it as a month and a day, not as a date
in the current year — the year it applies to depends on the period you are calculating.

## The offset carries meaning

On a recording — `start`, `end`, and the GPS `timestamp` — the offset is the one on the device the
entry was made on. It is not necessarily UTC, and it is not necessarily the account's time zone.

That makes it information, not formatting. A working time started at `08:00+02:00` was started at
eight in the morning where the person was. Convert it to UTC for storage and you can still show the
right instant, but you have lost what the clock on the wall said — which is usually the thing a
timesheet is about. Keep the offset you were given, and send back the offset that applies where the
recording happened.

Audit timestamps are different. `created`, `last_modified` and their kind are always UTC, and say
when the server acted. Do not infer a device time zone from them.

## Sending values

Send an explicit offset on every date-time you write. RFC 3339 requires one, and `Z` is accepted as
`+00:00`.

## Filtering by day

The filters that narrow a list to a period take plain dates and include both ends. `start_from` and
`start_to` on the recording lists select entries whose **start** falls on or after, and on or before,
the given day — so `start_from=2021-07-01&start_to=2021-07-31` returns everything that started in
July, including entries that run past midnight on the 31st.

Each filter says which property it applies to. `entry_date_from` and `resign_date_to` on the user
list work the same way against employment dates.

## Durations

Durations are **integer minutes**, never ISO 8601 durations. A working time, project time or drive
log carries a `duration` object rather than a bare number:

```json
{
  "duration": {
    "type": "minutes",
    "minutes": 42,
    "minutes_rounded": 45
  }
}
```

`minutes` is the net duration; `minutes_rounded` is the same value after the rounding rule the
account is configured with, which is what most reports and invoices are built on. Read whichever the
integration is meant to reflect, and do not recompute either from `start` and `end` — breaks are
already deducted from them.

`type` says how the duration is expressed. `minutes` is a measured stretch of time; `full_day` and
`half_day` are for absences booked by the day, where timr derives the minutes from the user's work
schedule rather than from a clock. You only send `duration_type` when the working time type is
recorded in days or half days.

Elsewhere, plain minute fields carry their unit in the name — `break_time_total_minutes`,
`target_duration_minutes`, `balance_total_minutes` — and are integers for the same reason.

tags.name: Pagination
tags.description:
List endpoints are cursor paginated. Ask for a page, and the response tells you how to get the next
one.

```http
GET /v1/working-times?limit=100 HTTP/1.1
```

```json
{
  "data": [ ... ],
  "next_page_token": "eyJpZCI6IjAxSFEzRjhYSzJSN1dZNU40TTZWVDlaQlFEIn0"
}
```

Pass that token back as `page_token` to continue, and keep going until `next_page_token` is `null`:

```http
GET /v1/working-times?limit=100&page_token=eyJpZCI6IjAxSFEzRjhYSzJSN1dZNU40TTZWVDlaQlFEIn0 HTTP/1.1
```

The `Link` header points at the same next page, if you would rather follow it than build the URL.

## What to expect

`limit` sizes the page. It defaults to 20, and values above 500 are capped at 500 rather than
rejected — so asking for a thousand gives you five hundred, not an error.

**There is no total count.** A cursor cannot know one without counting the whole result, so nothing
in the response tells you how many entries match. Do not build a page-number UI on top of this;
iterate until the token is `null`, or show a "load more" affordance.

Keep the other query parameters identical while you page. The token encodes where you stopped in a
particular result, and changing the filter underneath it makes the continuation meaningless.

An empty first page means nothing matched — or that the entries exist but the authenticated user or
client is not permitted to see them.

tags.name: Sorting
tags.description:
Pass `sort_by` to choose the property and `sort_direction` to choose the direction, `asc` or `dsc`:

```http
GET /v1/working-times?sort_by=start&sort_direction=dsc HTTP/1.1
```

Which properties an endpoint can sort by is part of its own description in the reference — they
differ, because they describe different things.

## Order is stable across pages

Every sort ends with the entry `id` as a tiebreaker. Without one, entries sharing a value could come
back in a different order on each request, and a cursor walking through them could show an entry
twice or skip it entirely. With one, the order is total, and paging through a large result is safe.

The tiebreaker is applied for you; you never pass it.

Sorting by `id` yourself is not meaningful — identifiers are opaque and their order says nothing
about the entries. Sort by a property that means something, such as `start` or `last_modified`.

tags.name: Deleted entries
tags.description:
An integration that keeps its own copy of timr data faces a problem the ordinary list endpoints
cannot solve: an entry that was deleted simply stops appearing, and nothing tells you it was ever
there.

Endpoints ending in `:deleted` close that gap. They list the entries that were deleted, so you can
remove them from your copy too:

```http
GET /v1/working-times:deleted HTTP/1.1
```

They return the `id`, along with `last_modified` and `last_modified_by` recording when the deletion
happened and who made it — not the original content, which is gone. Match the `id` against what you
hold and drop it.

## Reconciling

A sync that only ever adds and updates will drift. A complete pass is:

1. Fetch what changed since your last run from the ordinary list endpoint.
2. Fetch the deletions from the matching `:deleted` endpoint for the same period.
3. Apply both, and record when you ran.

Deleted entries are paginated and sorted like every other list, so the same rules apply — page until
`next_page_token` is `null`, and keep your filters identical while you do.

tags.name: User
tags.description: The people in the account who record times. A User holds identity and employment data and is assigned a Work Schedule Model and a Holiday Calendar. Working Times, Project Times and Drive Logs all belong to a User.

tags.name: Team
tags.description: Hierarchical groups of Users. Team membership and leadership determine who can see and manage whose records.

tags.name: Working Time
tags.description: Records that a person was at work, or absent — one continuous stretch from start to end, classified by its Working Time Type. Every balance timr derives starts here.

tags.name: Working Time Type
tags.description: The classification applied to a Working Time: attendance time, vacation, paid or unpaid time off, suspension, or break time. The type governs how the time counts toward balances and how breaks are deducted.

tags.name: Working Time Date Span
tags.description: A multi-day bracket around day-based Working Times of a single type, typically an absence such as vacation or sick leave. timr derives one Working Time per covered day, so the period is recorded once instead of day by day.

tags.name: Time Account
tags.description: The balances derived from a User's recordings — target against actual duration, overtime, and further accounts such as vacation. Read-only, and always evaluated as of a given day.

tags.name: Work Schedule Model
tags.description: Reusable templates defining the expected target duration per weekday. timr compares recorded Working Times against the assigned model to derive overtime and account balances.

tags.name: Holiday Calendar
tags.description: Named sets of public holidays assigned to Users. They determine the non-working days used when target hours and absences are calculated.

tags.name: Project Time
tags.description: Time booked on a Task. Where a Working Time records that a person was at work, a Project Time records what they worked on.

tags.name: Task
tags.description: The account's task tree that Project Times are booked on. Tasks are hierarchical, can be bookable and billable, carry budgets, and can constrain recording. Users gain access through assignments.

tags.name: Task to User Assignment
tags.description: Grants an individual User access to a Task, and controls whether they may currently record on it.

tags.name: Task to Leader Assignment
tags.description: Makes a User the leader of a Task, responsible for the records booked beneath it.

tags.name: Task to Team Assignment
tags.description: Grants a whole Team access to a Task, instead of assigning each of its Users individually.

tags.name: Drive Log
tags.description: Logbook entries for trips in a Car: times, mileage, purpose, places visited, and the category separating business from private travel.

tags.name: Drive Log Category
tags.description: Classifies a Drive Log, most importantly as business or private, for tax and reporting purposes.

tags.name: Car
tags.description: The vehicles that Drive Logs are recorded against.

tags.name: Track
tags.description: The recorded GPS route of a Drive Log. A Drive Log holds at most one Track.

OAuth2.description: OAuth2 authentication for the timr API. Use Client Credentials for machine-to-machine integrations in the client context, or Authorization Code with refresh tokens when the integration acts on behalf of a timr user. Unauthenticated responses advertise the API's RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata URL through the `WWW-Authenticate` header. The separate timr AuthServer publishes its OpenID Provider metadata at https://system.timr.com/id/.well-known/openid-configuration. Use this discovery document to obtain the current authorization and token endpoints instead of hardcoding them.

scopes.timrclient: Access timr data in the client context.

scopes.offline_access: Request a refresh token for continued access.

ProblemDetail.description: RFC 9457 Problem Details base members (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`) — the common shape of all error response bodies.

Error.description:
TIMR error response body, extending the Problem Details base with `timestamp`, `trace_id` and per-field `errors[]` for validation, binding, constraint, request-body deserialization, and reference-not-found errors. The semantic identifier is encoded in the `type` URI (e.g. `https://errors.timr.com/conflict/resource-outdated`).

Slugs in the `type` URI are lowercase kebab-case: a top-level category (`validation`, `reference-not-found`, `conflict`, `forbidden`, `internal`) optionally followed by a specific sub-slug (`conflict/resource-outdated`, `validation/end-time-required`, `reference-not-found/user`).

ErrorEntry.description: Field-level or sub-error entry, shaped like a sub-ProblemDetail. The `type` URI identifies the specific constraint or sub-error category (e.g. `validation/not-null` for a Bean Validation `@NotNull`, `validation/paused-working-time` for a TIMR custom validator code, `validation/type-mismatch` for a value that does not fit its target type, `validation/unknown-property` for a property the resource does not declare, `reference-not-found/user` for a `MappingException`). `field` is the JSONPath of the offending property in the request body, rooted at `$` — array elements included. An error about a query parameter names it plainly instead, without the `$.` prefix.

start.description: For WorkingTimeTypes with `edit_unit` `days` or `half_days`, `start` must be midnight (00:00) and on the same day as `end`. RFC 3339 date-time (ISO-8601)

end.description: For WorkingTimeTypes with `edit_unit` `days` or `half_days`, `end` must be midnight (00:00) and on the same day as `start`. RFC 3339 date-time (ISO-8601)

duration_type.description: Must be specified for WorkingTimeTypes with `edit_unit` `days` or `half_days` only

ProjectTimeStatus.description: Processing state of a Project Time. `running` and `paused` mean the recording is still open; from `changeable` on it is closed and progressively locked down as it is approved, cleared, closed and archived.

id.description: Unique identifier. Treat it as an opaque string.

breadcrumbs.description: Full path of the entry within its hierarchy, including its own name.

external_id.description: Identifier of the corresponding object in an external system. Set and owned by the client.

Task.description: A task, placed in the tree by `parent_task`, with the full path from the root in `breadcrumbs`. `bookable` and `billable` control recording and invoicing; `lock_date`, time windows and location constrain what may be recorded.

budget_update_project_times.description: this property is used to decide whether existing project times that have been booked to this task should be updated with the changed budget.  If budget_planning type or budget_hourly_rate are set, this property must also be set.   Based on this, the budgets of the existing project times are then recalculated or not.

parent_task_id.description: returns the id of the immediate parent task if the task has one. Use this id when creating or a updating a task in order to locate it at the right place in your task tree.

external_id.description: Identifier of the corresponding object in an external system. Set and owned by the client.

bookable.description: when a task is not bookable, no project times can be booked on it. You need to define child tasks, to book on tasks related to this task.

project_time_notes_required.description: depending on this property project times booked on this task have to include notes or not

start_date.description: the task is only available for selection after start_date, however, it can change if a lock_date is set and this is after the start_date. Furthermore, no booking of a project time with date < start or > end is possible.

end_date.description: the task is only available for selection before end_date, however, it can change if a lock_date is set and this is before the end_date. Furthermore, no booking of a project time with date < start or > end is possible.

lock_date.description:
with lock_date property you define a point in time before which existing entries can no longer be changed. This way you ensure that

  * existing entries cannot be changed or deleted
  * no entries can be added later

earliest_start_time.description: set this property to limit the task so that it cannot be booked before this time

latest_end_time.description: set this property to limit the task so that it cannot be booked after this time

budget_planning_type.description: when no budget is planned, either don't set this property (on create) or set it to none. set it to inherited to inherit budget settings from parent task.

budget_hours_planned.description:
how many hours were planned in the calculation
set budget_hours_planned to make timr calculate budget_planned depending on its budget_planning_type:
  * task_hourly_rate: out of budget_hourly_rate and budget_planned
  * user_hourly_rate: out of fixed hours budget (employee budget) and budget_hours_planned
  * fixed_price: out of budget_hourly_rate and budget_planned

budget_hourly_rate.description:
depending on its budget_planning_type this property may or may not be set:
  * **task_hourly_rate: this property is necessary to calculate budgets, by default it will be set to 0.00**
  * **user_hourly_rate: this property cannot be set**
  * fixed_price: you can set this property if you want to make timr calculate budget_hours_planned or budget_planned based on its value

budget_planned.description:
the price at which the task was sold
set budget_planned to make timr calculate the budget_hours_planned depending on its budget_planning_type:
  * task_hourly_rate: out of budget_hourly_rate and budget_planned
  * user_hourly_rate: out of fixed hours budget (employee budget) and budget_planned
  * fixed_price: out of budget_hourly_rate and budget_planned

budget_include_non_billable_project_time.description: set this property to true, if you want to include not billable hours for all project times booked on this task

location_inherited.description: set this property to false if you want to set a child task's location explicitly instead of inheriting it from its parent

location_restriction_radius_meters.description: set this property to make recording of project times for this task via the app on the smartphone only possible within this defined geofence radius

custom_field_1.description: you can configure custom fields for tasks in the settings of timr under Administration/Settings/Tasks. To add a new custom field, simply choose a name for the field.

custom_field_2.description: you can configure custom fields for tasks in the settings of timr under Administration/Settings/Tasks. To add a new custom field, simply choose a name for the field.

custom_field_3.description: you can configure custom fields for tasks in the settings of timr under Administration/Settings/Tasks. To add a new custom field, simply choose a name for the field.

TaskLocation.description: You can define the location of a task by setting this property. If the task has a parent task, the location is inherited if nothing else is explicitly defined. If you set this property to null, the location will be deleted.

TasksSortColumn.description: Sort property for Tasks. `breadcrumbs` orders by the Task's full path, `name` by its own name only.

TaskToUserAssignmentsSortColumn.description: Sort property for Task to User Assignments. `user_name` orders by the assigned User's last name, then first name.

RecordingLockType.description: Whether the assigned User may record on the Task, and where the lock comes from. `recordable` allows recording; `locked_automatically` follows the Task's lock date; `locked_manually` and `unlocked_manually` are explicit overrides for this assignment.

BudgetPlanningType.description:
corresponding to the chosen planning type some properties cannot be set:
  * none: no further budget properties can be set
  * user_hourly_rate: budget_hourly_rate cannot be set

for the remaining two types all budget properties are supported

BudgetPlanningTypeRequest.description:
corresponding to the chosen planning type some properties cannot be set:
  * none: no further budget properties can be set
  * user_hourly_rate: budget_hourly_rate cannot be set
  * inherited: budget settings are inherited from the parent task

for the remaining two types all budget properties are supported

TaskToLeaderAssignmentsSortColumn.description: Sort property for Task to Leader Assignments. `user_name` orders by the assigned User's last name, then first name.

TaskToTeamAssignmentsSortColumn.description: Sort property for Task to Team Assignments. `team_name` orders by the assigned Team's name.
